chapters.title: Chapter 5: Agri Commodities and Base Metals

lessons.title: Agri Commodities on NCDEX: Seasonality, Monsoons and Supply Cycles

children.text: A trader in Unjha does not start the day by reading the Nifty. He checks arrivals at the mandi, the weather in north Gujarat and Rajasthan, and whether the government has said anything about exports. Agri commodities run on a completely different clock from gold and crude: the clock of sowing, rain, harvest and storage. Prices can double in a season because of a weak monsoon and halve the next year because every farmer planted the same crop. By the end of this lesson you will understand India's kharif and rabi cycles, how the monsoon feeds into prices, why prices tend to be lowest at harvest, and how to read the supply cycle behind contracts like jeera, guar seed, castor seed, turmeric and coriander on NCDEX.

body.text: Agri prices are set by one harvest at a time. Supply is fixed once the crop is in the ground, so everything that happens between sowing and the next harvest, especially rain, shows up in price.

children.text: The Monsoon: India's Most Important Weather Event

The southwest monsoon, from June to September, brings the large majority of India's annual rainfall. Its timing, total quantity and distribution across states decide how much kharif crop gets sown, how well it grows, and how much moisture remains in the soil and reservoirs for rabi.

markDefs.definition: The average all-India southwest monsoon rainfall over a 50-year reference period, used by IMD as the benchmark for normal. For 1971 to 2020 it is about 87 cm.

children.text: The India Meteorological Department (IMD) measures monsoon rainfall against the
long period average
(LPA), which is about 87 cm for June to September.

body.latex: \text{Monsoon rainfall as \% of LPA} = \frac{\text{Actual June to September rainfall}}{\text{Long period average}} \times 100
body.caption: IMD issues forecasts in this form, typically a first forecast in April and an update around late May or June.
IMD categories for all-India monsoon rainfall

body.title: Classify the monsoon
body.prompt: Actual all-India June to September rainfall is 800 mm, and the long period average is 868.6 mm. What is the rainfall as a percentage of LPA, rounded to one decimal place?
body.explanation: 800 ÷ 868.6 × 100 = 92.1%. That falls in the "below normal" band of 90% to 95%. For agri traders, the next question is where the shortfall happened, because a deficit over Rajasthan matters far more for guar than a deficit over the northeast.

body.text: The all-India number hides what matters. A "normal" monsoon can still mean drought in western Rajasthan and floods in Maharashtra. Agri traders watch state and district-level rainfall and the weekly sowing progress reports from the Ministry of Agriculture, not just the headline percentage.

children.text: The Seasonal Price Pattern

markDefs.definition: The quantity of a crop brought to mandis for sale. Heavy arrivals after harvest usually pressure prices, and thin arrivals in the lean season usually support them.

children.text: Once a crop is harvested, a large volume hits the mandis at once. These heavy
arrivals

usually pressure prices. As the months pass, stocks are used up, carrying costs build, and traders start watching the next crop. Prices often firm up through the lean season, until news of the next crop arrives.

body.title: Illustrative seasonal tendency for a rabi spice like jeera (price index, February = 100)

body.text: Seasonality is a tendency, not a timetable. In years with a crop failure, prices can rise straight through the harvest season. In years with a bumper crop and large carry-over stocks, the "lean season rally" may never come. Always weigh the season against the actual supply picture.

children.text: The seasonal rise is not free money. Someone who buys at harvest and sells months later has to pay for storage, insurance and the interest on the money tied up, the same cost of carry you learned about in Chapter 2.

body.title: Is the seasonal carry worth it?
body.prompt: A stockist in Unjha buys 50 quintals of jeera at harvest for ₹22,000 per quintal and sells 7 months later at ₹26,500. Storage costs ₹60 per quintal per month, and the money tied up costs 10% a year in interest. What is the net profit on the 50 quintals, to the nearest rupee?
body.explanation: Gross gain = ₹26,500 minus ₹22,000 = ₹4,500 per quintal. Storage = ₹60 × 7 = ₹420. Interest = ₹22,000 × 10% × 7 ÷ 12 = ₹1,283.33. Net = ₹4,500 minus ₹420 minus ₹1,283.33 = ₹2,796.67 per quintal. × 50 = ₹1,39,833. The carrying costs ate about 38% of the gross gain.

children.text: Sown area.
Weekly sowing data tells traders early whether farmers have expanded or cut a crop.
Carry-over stocks.
Stock left from last season can cushion a poor crop or deepen a glut.
Export demand.
India is a major exporter of spices like jeera and of castor oil, so overseas demand matters, including from China and the Gulf.
Industrial demand.
Guar gum demand depends on the US oil and gas drilling cycle; castor oil demand depends on chemical and lubricant industries.
Government policy.
Export bans, stock limits under the Essential Commodities Act, import duty changes and MSP decisions can reset prices quickly.

body.label: Minimum support price
body.value: A floor for some crops, not for most NCDEX spices
body.context: The government announces MSPs for 22 mandated crops, such as paddy, wheat and pulses. Commodities like jeera, coriander, guar seed and turmeric are not on that list, so their prices can fall much further in a glut.

children.text: The Supply Cycle: Why Booms Plant Busts

markDefs.definition: A recurring boom and bust pattern in farm markets: high prices lead farmers to plant more, which creates a glut and low prices, which leads them to plant less, and so on.

children.text: Farmers decide what to sow largely based on the prices they recently received. That creates a recurring pattern, sometimes called the
cobweb cycle
High prices this season.
A poor crop sends prices to record levels.
Farmers plant more.
Attracted by those prices, farmers shift acreage into the crop for the next season.
A big harvest arrives.
With normal weather, the larger area produces a bumper crop.
Prices crash.
Supply overwhelms demand, and prices fall sharply.
Farmers plant less.
Burned by low prices, they switch to other crops, setting up the next shortage.

body.title: A recent example: jeera in 2023 and 2024

children.text: Jeera is a textbook case of this cycle.
2022 to 2023: lower sowing and weather damage in Gujarat and Rajasthan cut supply. Jeera prices climbed to record levels, above ₹60,000 per quintal in 2023.
2023 to 2024 rabi season: attracted by those prices, farmers sharply expanded jeera sowing.
2024: a much larger crop arrived, and prices fell by more than half from their peak.
A trader who understood the cycle would have watched the 2023 to 2024 sowing data very closely. The record prices were themselves the signal that supply was about to respond.

children.text: Quality matters.
Delivery requires produce that meets the contract grade, tested at accredited warehouses. Off-grade produce may be rejected or accepted at a discount.
Liquidity varies.
Many agri contracts are far less liquid than MCX gold or crude, with wider bid-ask spreads.
Policy risk is higher.
Food commodities are politically sensitive, and trading in some contracts has been suspended. The last lesson of this chapter covers why.

body.title: Which crop watches the monsoon most?
body.question: In early July, IMD reports that monsoon rainfall over western Rajasthan is far below normal. Which NCDEX commodity's supply outlook is most directly affected?
body.explanation: Guar is a kharif crop sown in July, concentrated in western Rajasthan and heavily dependent on monsoon rain. Jeera, coriander and mustard are rabi crops sown after the monsoon, affected more indirectly through soil moisture.

body.title: Harvest pressure
body.textWithBlank: After harvest, heavy mandi ___ usually put pressure on agri prices.
body.explanation: Arrivals are the quantity of produce brought to mandis. When they peak after harvest, supply is at its most plentiful and prices often soften.

body.title: The weak monsoon trade
body.scenario: Mahesh, a 44-year-old commission agent in Jodhpur, reads in mid-June that IMD expects below-normal rainfall over northwest India. He wants to buy NCDEX guar seed futures immediately, sure that a weak monsoon means a small crop and higher prices.
body.prompt: What else should Mahesh check before trading, and what could go wrong with his reasoning?
body.modelAnswer:
What to check:
1. Distribution and timing. A forecast for "northwest India" is broad. What matters is actual rainfall in western Rajasthan in July, when guar is sown. A late but adequate burst of rain can still allow good sowing.
2. Sowing data. Weekly sown area reports will show whether farmers are planting more or less guar than last year.
3. Carry-over stocks. Large stocks from previous seasons can cap any price rise.
4. Demand. Guar gum demand depends heavily on the US oil and gas drilling cycle. Weak drilling can offset a small crop.
5. Contract month and liquidity. He should choose a contract that reflects the new crop, and check volume, open interest and price limits.

What could go wrong: forecasts change, the market may already have priced in the weak monsoon, and farmers facing poor rain sometimes switch to hardy crops like guar, which could increase guar area rather than cut it. A trade based on a single forecast headline, without sowing and demand data, is a guess.

Produce brought to mandis for sale; heavy arrivals after harvest usually pressure prices.

points: Kharif crops follow the June to September monsoon; rabi crops are sown after it and harvested in spring.
IMD measures the monsoon against the long period average; 96% to 104% is normal and below 90% is deficient.
Prices often soften at harvest when arrivals peak and firm through the lean season, but crop size can override the pattern.
Seasonal gains must cover storage and interest, the same cost of carry that shapes futures prices.
The cobweb cycle means record prices often lead to more planting and a later crash, as jeera showed in 2023 and 2024.
NCDEX agri contracts depend on quality, delivery centres, liquidity and policy, not just price views.

body.text: This lesson is for education only and is not investment advice. Crop calendars, seasonal patterns and delivery centres are typical and vary by region and year. Historical price references are approximate. Agri commodity derivatives can be illiquid and are subject to regulatory action. Commodity derivatives are leveraged and can cause losses larger than your initial margin.
